title: Leaders Can Put Too Much Faith in Personality Diagnostics
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece cautions against over-reliance on personality assessments and psychometrics in hiring, arguing that leaders can slide from using these tools as useful data points into treating them as a definitive litmus test. The author identifies confirmation bias as the mechanism that sustains this overreach. The piece argues that experience, skill, and self-awareness matter more than personality in predicting who will actually succeed. It closes on the honest admission that the most reliable prediction leaders can make about any new hire is that they will surprise everyone.
points: Leaders often slide from using personality assessments as one useful data point into treating them as a definitive litmus test for hiring.
Confirmation bias sustains this overreach, once a leader believes a diagnostic accurately predicts success, they rationalize its failures.
The piece explicitly ranks factors, arguing experience, skill, and self-awareness matter more than personality assessments.
The closing admission is that the most reliable prediction about any new hire is that they will surprise leaders, for better or worse.
quotes: This makes good sense — until the leader or recruiting team becomes convinced that only candidates with the “right” predictors should be considered for selection.
Because of the complexity associated with human behavior, especially experience, drive, passion, and learning, the predictive power of personality, or any set of psychometrics, is limited.

The confirmation bias associated with this belief is well-known. Once a leader convinces themselves that a diagnostic can accurately predict success, they rationalize why many predictions fail to deliver over time.
Personality matters, but not more than experience, skill, and self-awareness.
In reality, the most accurate prediction leaders can make about prospective hires is that they will confound description. New hires will always surprise leaders, in both good and bad ways.
